apps.name: PulseFast
apps.status: Available on the App Store · Android coming soon
apps.summary: PulseFast is a fasting companion. Start and stop a fast with one tap, watch a live ring close in on your goal, and keep every session, note and insight in one place — without a spreadsheet. It handles everyday intermittent fasting and longer extended fasts alike.
long: Pick a preset — 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 or 72 hours — or set a custom target anywhere from 12 hours to 168 hours (7 days). PulseFast tracks the fasting window and the eating window that follows it, so you never have to do the arithmetic yourself.

When you close a fast you can attach a note: how hunger went, what you ate, what got in the way. Over time those notes turn into insight cards — rolling averages, longest fast, eating-window quality and a running tally of goals met.
On iOS a Live Activity keeps the countdown on your Lock Screen, and a home screen widget shows current progress on both platforms.

PulseFast does not endorse or recommend any specific fasting duration. The presets are provided for convenience only, and the app shows a health disclaimer before you commit to a long fast. Consult a healthcare professional to decide what is safe and appropriate for you.
features: One-tap fasting
Start or stop instantly. Eating windows are captured automatically the moment a fast closes.
Presets and custom goals
Presets from 13 to 72 hours out of the box, plus any custom target from 12 hours up to 168 hours (7 days).
Live progress ring
A goal ring that updates in real time, mirrored on the home screen widget and iOS Lock Screen.
Session journaling
Attach hunger, meal and context notes to each closed fast so patterns are readable later.
Hydration and activity
Log hydration in-app, and optionally read steps, distance and active energy from Apple Health or Health Connect.
Insights and history
Rolling averages, longest fast, eating-window quality and a full timestamped history you can export.

privacy.headline: PulseFast keeps your fasting data on your device. There are no accounts, no analytics and no servers.

To tell you when a fasting window opens or closes. Reminders are scheduled on your device; nothing is sent through a push server.
Run at startup
So reminders you already scheduled survive a device restart.
Apple Health / Health Connect — read (optional)
If you grant it, PulseFast reads steps, walking distance and active energy to show activity next to your fast. It is never required, and the app works fully without it.
Apple Health / Health Connect — write (optional)
If you grant it, hydration and calories you log in PulseFast can be saved back to Health so your other apps can see them.
privacy.network: PulseFast has no backend. It does not send your fasting data, health data or notes anywhere. If you use the export or share feature, the file goes wherever you send it — that destination's own privacy terms then apply.
privacy.third_parties: None. There are no analytics SDKs, advertising libraries, crash reporters or trackers in the app.
privacy.health_note: Health data is treated as sensitive. PulseFast reads it only with your explicit permission, uses it only to display activity inside the app, and never transmits it off your device or uses it for advertising.

faq: Which fasting schedules are supported?
Presets at 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 and 72 hours, plus any custom target between 12 and 168 hours (7 days).
Do I need an account?
No. There is no sign-up and no login. The app works fully offline.
Is Health integration required?
No. Apple Health and Health Connect are both optional. Decline the permission and every other feature still works.
Where is my data stored?
On your device only. Deleting the app removes its local data, subject to your device's own backup and restore settings.
Can I get my data out?
Yes — export your history from the app and send it wherever you like via the standard share sheet.
Which platforms are supported?
iPhone, on the App Store now, including Live Activities on the Lock Screen. The Android version is coming to Google Play.

apps.name: LucidCapture
apps.status: Available on the Mac App Store
apps.summary: LucidCapture is a screenshot tool that lives in your menu bar and stays out of your way. Press a key, grab what you need, mark it up, and get on with your work.
long: Capture a region, a single window or a whole display from a global shortcut — ⌃⇧3, ⌃⇧4 and ⌃⇧5 out of the box, remappable to whatever you prefer. Window captures come out with a proper macOS drop shadow and padding, so they look finished without extra work.

Every capture lands in your clipboard immediately and appears as a floating thumbnail you can click to edit or drag straight into another app. Annotations — arrows, boxes, highlights, text labels and crops — stay editable rather than being baked into the pixels.
Redaction is real redaction: the covered pixels are destroyed in the exported image, not painted over with a rectangle someone can move aside.
features: Menu bar, no dock icon
Launches instantly, does no idle work, and never takes up a slot in your dock.
Global shortcuts
Region, window and display capture from the keyboard, with remappable hotkeys.
Zero-click flow
Capture, auto-copy to clipboard, floating thumbnail — click to edit, drag to drop the file elsewhere.
Editable annotations
Arrows, boxes, highlights, text and crop. Move, re-edit or delete anything you have already drawn.
Proper redaction
Redacted pixels are destroyed in the export, not merely covered.
Searchable library
A keyboard-navigable grid of past captures with Quick Look, search, drag-out and Reveal in Finder.

privacy.headline: LucidCapture collects nothing. It ships sandboxed with no networking entitlement, so it is technically incapable of making a network connection at all.

So the library is still there next launch
An index file in the same container
macOS user defaults on this Mac
To remember how you like the app configured
A bookmark to your chosen save folder
macOS user defaults on this Mac
Only if you turn on “Also save to folder”, so it can keep writing there after a restart
permissions: Screen Recording
macOS requires this permission of any app that captures the screen. LucidCapture uses it solely to take the screenshots you ask for, when you ask for them. Nothing is captured in the background.
Folder access (optional)
Only the one folder you pick yourself through the standard macOS panel, and only if you enable saving copies to a folder.
privacy.network: None, and this is enforced rather than promised: the app ships without the network entitlement, so macOS itself blocks any outgoing or incoming connection whether or not the code attempts one. There is no server for your screenshots to go to.
privacy.third_parties: None. No third-party SDKs, advertising libraries, trackers or analytics frameworks are compiled into the app.
privacy.extra: LucidCapture does not request access to your camera, microphone, location, contacts, calendars or photo library, and cannot read any file you have not explicitly opened.

faq: Why does macOS ask for Screen Recording permission?
macOS requires it of every screenshot app without exception. Grant it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen Recording, then relaunch LucidCapture.
Do my screenshots leave my Mac?
No. The app has no network entitlement, so it cannot make a connection at all.
Can I change the keyboard shortcuts?
Yes, in Settings. The defaults are ⌃⇧3 for display, ⌃⇧4 for region and ⌃⇧5 for window.
Where are my captures stored?
In the app's own sandbox container. You can also turn on “Also save to folder” and pick a folder of your own.
Is redaction actually safe?
Yes. Redacted regions are destroyed in the exported image rather than covered by a shape that could be removed.
How do I remove everything the app has stored?
Delete captures from inside the library, or remove the app and its container to clear all of its data at once.

apps.name: SyntaxPad
apps.tagline: A fast, native Mac text editor.
apps.status: Available on the Mac App Store
apps.summary: SyntaxPad is a lightweight, native macOS editor for notes, code, configuration files and Markdown — built entirely on Apple frameworks, with no Electron and no web runtime.
long: It is not trying to replace Xcode or VS Code. It is the editor you reach for to open a config file, jot a note, read someone else's source, or write Markdown — and it opens instantly, every time.
Tabs, syntax highlighting, a background find-and-replace that will not freeze on a pathological regex, and a Markdown preview that renders locally under a strict content security policy.
Your unsaved scratch tabs survive a quit. Your open files come back where you left them.
features: Native and fast
100% AppKit and SwiftUI. No Electron, no bundled browser, no cross-platform runtime.
Tabs and session restore
Unsaved scratch tabs and window state come back next launch.
Syntax highlighting
For source files, configuration formats and Markdown.
Find and replace
Runs on a background queue behind a debounce, so a slow regex cannot hang the app.
Local Markdown preview
Rendered on your Mac under a strict CSP that blocks scripts and network requests entirely.
Large files
Built to stay responsive on files that make lighter editors struggle.

privacy.headline: SyntaxPad collects no data. No accounts, no analytics, no telemetry, no crash reporting, no advertising, and it makes no network requests. Your documents never leave your Mac.
stored: Wherever you choose to save them
Unsaved scratch tabs and window state
So your tabs are still there next launch
To populate the Open Recent menu
To remember how you like the editor
Security-scoped bookmarks for files you opened
So files reopen after a restart without asking again
permissions: Files you choose yourself

SyntaxPad runs in the macOS App Sandbox with four entitlements — app sandbox, user-selected file read/write, app-scope bookmarks, and the network-client entitlement that macOS requires before it will start the web-rendering component behind the Markdown preview. It can read and write only files you have picked through an Open or Save dialog.
privacy.network: None. SyntaxPad makes no network requests — there is no server to contact and no code that contacts one. It does declare the network-client entitlement, but not to reach the network: macOS will not start the system web-rendering component behind the Markdown preview without it. That preview is served under a `default-src 'none'` content security policy, which is what actually prevents a Markdown file loading a remote image, phoning home, or reporting that you opened it. Remote images therefore show their alt text instead — a deliberate trade.
privacy.third_parties: None. No SDKs, no trackers, no analytics.
privacy.extra: Links you click in a Markdown preview open in your default browser, and only http, https and mailto links are permitted. Once a link opens, that browser's own privacy policy applies.

faq: Why don't remote images appear in the Markdown preview?
The preview blocks all network requests by design, so a document cannot signal that you opened it. Alt text is shown instead.
Can SyntaxPad open files anywhere on my Mac?
Only files you pick through an Open or Save dialog. The sandbox blocks everything else.
Are my unsaved tabs safe if I quit?
Yes. Scratch tabs and window state are saved into the app's container and restored on next launch.
Does it work offline?
Always — it has no network access at all.
How do I remove everything it has stored?
Delete the app and its sandbox container. Documents you saved yourself are untouched, since they are your own files.

apps.name: Black Hole Rush
apps.summary: A fast-session arcade growth game. You are a small black hole loose in Gravity City. Everything you swallow makes you bigger, and everything bigger than you is a threat — until it isn't.
long: A match runs two minutes across three phases — Scavenge, Expansion and Collapse — and then a thirty-second sudden-death Elimination round where a single point of mass is enough to swallow a rival and nobody who goes down comes back.
Six seeded districts, five personality-driven bots, and capture rules that are exactly as strict as they sound: you need a 0.1% radius edge, so only a near-exact tie bounces.
Everything unlockable is cosmetic. There is no pay-to-win system, no energy gate and no timer standing between you and the next match — rematch happens without a reload.
features: Three-minute sessions
A two-minute three-phase match plus a thirty-second elimination round. Built for the gap between other things.
Six districts
Gravity City is seeded into six districts with different object density and risk.
Five rival bots
Each with its own personality — they hunt, hoard and avoid differently.
Gravity Pulse
A short-cooldown ability that shoves nearby mass, on a button and on the space bar.
Cosmetics only
Progression, challenges and equippable cosmetics. No pay-to-win, no loot boxes, no energy gates.
Accessibility
Reduced motion, high contrast, text size, handedness, camera shake, and separate music, effects and haptics controls.

apps.name: ClipVault
apps.tagline: Private clipboard history for your Mac.
apps.summary: ClipVault is a clipboard manager that lives in your menu bar. Copy as you normally would; when you need something again, press ⌘⇧V, type a few letters and press Return. Your history never leaves your Mac.
long: ClipVault keeps what you copy — plain and rich text, links, images and references to files — and pastes it back in its original formats. Press ⌘⇧V, or a shortcut of your own, and the history window opens over whatever you are working in. Results narrow as you type, and filters such as type:image, app:Safari and is:pinned get you to the right item faster.

It is built for the keyboard. Arrow keys move, Return pastes, Shift-Return pastes as plain text, ⌘1–⌘9 pick from the top of the list, ⌘P pins and ⌘⌫ deletes. Pinned items are kept however old they get; everything else follows the limits you set, by count and by age.

You decide what it keeps. Pause capture from the menu bar whenever you like, and name apps it must never read from. Optional sensitive-content protection checks each copy in memory, before anything is saved, for one-time codes, card-like numbers, private keys, authentication codes, labelled secrets and password-manager content. It is off by default, every category is your choice, and it is a convenience rather than a guarantee — to be certain an app is never captured, exclude it.
features: Menu bar, no Dock icon
Opens from ⌘⇧V or the menu bar icon. A Dock icon is a setting away if you want one.
Every kind of copy
Text, rich text, links, images and file references, pasted back in their original formats.
Search as you type
Results narrow with every letter. Filter by kind with type:, by source with app:, or show only is:pinned.
Keyboard-first
Return pastes, Shift-Return pastes plain text, ⌘1–⌘9 pick from the top of the list, ⌘P pins, ⌘⌫ deletes.
Pins and limits
Pinned items stay put. Everything else is trimmed to your limits — 1,000 items and 30 days unless you change them.
You choose what is kept
Pause capture at any time, never capture from apps you name, and optionally skip sensitive content.

privacy.headline: ClipVault collects nothing. Your clipboard history is stored only on your Mac, and the app ships sandboxed with no network entitlement, so it is technically incapable of making a network connection at all.
stored: Your clipboard history: text, rich text, links, images and references to files you copy
A database and asset folder in the app's sandbox container on your Mac
So you can search it and paste from it again
The name of the app each item was copied from, and when
To show where an item came from, and for app: searches
So apps you exclude stay excluded
macOS user defaults on this Mac
To remember how you like the app configured
permissions: Paste from Other Apps

Reading the clipboard is what a clipboard manager does. On macOS 15.4 and later, if your Mac is set to ask before apps read the clipboard, ClipVault stops reading automatically and explains how to allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Paste from Other Apps.
Accessibility (optional)

Used only to send a single ⌘V to the app you are working in, after you choose an item. ClipVault does not use it to read other apps or to monitor your keystrokes. Decline it and ClipVault copies the item instead, and you press ⌘V yourself.
Launch at login (optional)
The setup screen offers a “Launch ClipVault at login” checkbox, ticked by default; untick it to decline. Change it later in Settings → General.
Choosing apps to exclude
Adding an app to Never Capture From opens the standard macOS panel, limited to applications and read-only. It is used only to learn which app you picked.
privacy.network: None, and this is enforced rather than promised: ClipVault ships sandboxed without the network entitlement, so macOS itself blocks any outgoing or incoming connection whether or not the code attempts one. There is no account, no sync and no server for your clipboard to go to.
privacy.third_parties: None. ClipVault is built only on Apple's own frameworks and the SQLite library that ships with macOS. No third-party SDKs, advertising libraries, trackers, analytics or crash reporters are compiled into the app.
privacy.extra: ClipVault never writes clipboard contents to the system log. By default it skips copies that other apps mark as transient or auto-generated, and it keeps its history out of Time Machine backups so that items you clear do not linger there — you can include it under Settings → Storage. It does not request access to your camera, microphone, location, contacts, calendars or photo library.

faq: How do I open my clipboard history?
Press ⌘⇧V, or choose Open Clipboard History from the ClipVault menu bar icon. You can change the shortcut in Settings → Shortcuts.
Why does macOS ask about Accessibility?

Only for pasting straight into the app you are working in: ClipVault sends a single ⌘V after you choose an item. Allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility, or skip it — ClipVault then copies the item and you press ⌘V yourself.
Why isn't ClipVault recording what I copy?

Check that capture isn't paused (the menu bar icon shows Resume Capture when it is) and that the app you copied from isn't under Never Capture From. On macOS 15.4 and later, also allow ClipVault in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Paste from Other Apps. Copies an app marks as temporary are skipped by default, and two copies made within about half a second of each other can register as one.
Why has ⌘⇧V stopped working as Paste and Match Style?
Some apps use ⌘⇧V for Paste and Match Style. While ClipVault holds that shortcut those apps won't receive it; pick a different one in Settings → Shortcuts.
Does my clipboard history leave my Mac?
No. The app has no network entitlement, so it cannot make a connection at all. History is also kept out of Time Machine backups unless you turn that on.
Is sensitive-content protection a guarantee?

No. It recognises common patterns — one-time codes, card-like numbers, private keys and the like — but it can miss things and occasionally flag ordinary text. To be certain an app is never captured, add it to Never Capture From.
How do I delete my history?
Choose Clear History from the menu bar icon, or use Settings → Storage, which can also clear just images. Delete single items with ⌘⌫ in the history window. Clearing takes effect immediately.

apps.name: Pixcelate
apps.tagline: Background removal that never leaves your phone.
apps.summary: Pixcelate lifts the subject out of a photo and hands you a clean transparent PNG. The segmentation model is bundled inside the app and runs on your own device, so there is no upload, no queue and no account — and it works in airplane mode.
long: Most background removers recognise a fixed list of things — people, cars, a handful of animals — and give up on anything else. Pixcelate uses a salient object model instead, which finds whatever the subject of the photo actually is without needing to name it. A plate of food, a pair of earrings, a houseplant, a signature on paper: all of them cut out the same way.

The cutout keeps a soft edge. Rather than deciding each pixel is in or out, the model produces a continuous matte that becomes the alpha channel directly — so hair, fur, blades of grass and motion blur survive instead of turning into a jagged sticker outline.

From there it is a proper editor. Eight filter presets, brightness, contrast, saturation and hue, blur, sharpen and clarity, rotation and aspect crop, and a background you can leave transparent or fill with a colour or gradient. Every change is non-destructive with twenty steps of undo, and you export as PNG or JPEG at full resolution or a size you choose.
features: Works on any subject
A salient object model finds the subject without needing to recognise it, so food, products, plants and documents all work — not just people and pets.
Soft edges, not stickers
The matte is used as a continuous alpha channel rather than an in-or-out mask, so hair, fur and grass keep their detail.
Entirely on device
The 2.4 MB model ships inside the app. Nothing is uploaded, there is no account, and removal works with no connection at all.
Live Photo aware
Pick a Live Photo and Pixcelate pulls out candidate frames, ranks them by sharpness and matches Apple's own key photo so you start from the right still.
Non-destructive editing
Presets, colour and detail adjustments, crop, rotate and background fill — all re-editable, with twenty steps of undo and redo.
Export on your terms
PNG to keep transparency or JPEG to save space, at full resolution or a maximum edge you pick, straight to your photo library or out through the share sheet.

privacy.headline: Pixcelate collects nothing. Your photos are processed by a model bundled inside the app, on your own device — there is no account, no backend and no analytics. On Android this is enforced rather than promised: the release build does not request the INTERNET permission, so the system itself blocks any connection.
stored: Your device's photo library, in a Pixcelate album
Because you tapped Save — this is the only thing the app deliberately keeps
A photo you take inside the app
Your device's photo library, and the app's temporary folder while you work on it
So you can cut it out; the working copy is swept once it is a day old
Working files — an extracted Live Photo frame, the file handed to the share sheet
The app's own temporary folder on your device
So a cutout survives long enough to be shared or saved; swept automatically once it is a day old
A diagnostic log, only if something goes wrong
The app's own temporary folder on your device
So you can read the error under Diagnostics and paste it into a bug report; swept on the same schedule
permissions: Photo library (read)
To open the photo or Live Photo you pick. Pixcelate only ever receives the single item you chose in the system picker — it cannot browse your library.
Camera (optional)

Only when you choose “Take a photo” instead of picking from your library. Pixcelate never opens the camera on its own, records nothing, and keeps the shot on your device like any other photo. Decline it and the library still works.
Photo library (add)
Only when you tap Save, to write the finished image into a Pixcelate album. Decline it and everything else still works; use the share sheet instead.
Storage on older Android (optional)
Android 10 and below required this to write a saved image to shared storage. It is capped at API 29 and is never requested on newer versions of Android.
privacy.network: None. There is no networking code in the app, no analytics, advertising, crash-reporting or attribution SDK, and no server for anything to be sent to. Background removal runs against a model file compiled into the app itself, which is why it behaves identically in airplane mode. On Android the release build declares no INTERNET permission at all, so Android blocks any connection whether or not code attempts one.
privacy.third_parties: None. No third-party SDK, advertising library, tracker or analytics framework is compiled into the app. The open-source components it does use — the system image picker, the TensorFlow Lite runtime, the share sheet and the photo-library writer — all run locally, and none of them report anything to anyone.
privacy.store_note: One qualification, for completeness: the development and profile builds used while the app is being written do declare Android's INTERNET permission, because Flutter's hot-reload tooling needs it. That permission is absent from the release build, which is the only build that ever reaches a store or a phone.
privacy.extra: Nothing you do in the editor survives closing the app. The cutout, the adjustments and the undo history are all held in memory only — quit Pixcelate and they are gone, and only what you deliberately exported to your photo library remains. Pixcelate does not request your microphone, location, contacts or calendars.

faq: Do my photos leave my device?

No. The segmentation model is bundled inside the app and runs locally. There is no server involved, and on Android the release build has no INTERNET permission, so a connection is not possible in the first place.
Does it work without a connection?
Yes, completely. Try it in airplane mode — nothing changes.
Does the camera shortcut record anything?
No. Choosing “Take a photo” opens the standard camera for a single shot, which is then handed to the editor. Pixcelate captures no video or audio, and never opens the camera unless you ask it to.
It cut out the wrong thing. What now?

Pixcelate looks for the single most prominent subject in the frame. On a scene with no clear subject — an open landscape, or a flat-lay of many objects — the result can be unpredictable. Cropping tighter around what you want before removing the background usually fixes it.
What happens when I pick a Live Photo?

Pixcelate pulls several still frames out of it, ranks them by sharpness, and compares them against Apple's own key photo so it can preselect the right one. You can override the choice, or ask for the key photo directly.
Where do saved photos go?
Into a Pixcelate album in your normal photo library. The Save confirmation has a View button that opens it.
How do I remove everything the app has stored?

Delete the exported photos from your photo library as you would any others, and delete the app. Its temporary working files go with it — and they are cleared automatically a day after they are written anyway.

apps.name: Twister Rush
apps.tagline: Twelve tiers, from drink cups to skyscrapers.
apps.summary: A 3D arcade tornado-growth game. Drive a funnel through a city, absorb everything you are big enough to lift, and climb a twelve-tier ladder from drink cups to skyscrapers.
long: What you can absorb is decided by how big an object actually is — measured off its mesh rather than read from a category someone assigned — so two things the same size always behave the same way, and a bigger thing is always harder.

Objects one tier above you do not sit still. They heave up, tip toward the funnel and drop back, and every so often one gives way. When one will not go, you can knock it flat instead — and a felled object needs 20% less tornado when you come back for it.
Five AI tornadoes share the city, colour-coded by archetype, and a crown floats over whichever funnel is currently the biggest, so you always know whether that is you.
features: Twelve-tier ladder
From drink cups to skyscrapers, with absorption decided by real mesh size.
Two-minute matches
A 3·2·1·GO countdown, a two-minute match, a ranked results screen and Play Again with no menu in between.
Five rival tornadoes
Colour-coded AI archetypes that hunt, harvest and avoid differently.
Objects that resist
Buildings heave and tip before they go. Knock one flat and it is easier next time.
The crown
Floats over the biggest tornado on the map so the standings are always readable at a glance.
One codebase, two stores
A single Unity project targeting iPhone, iPad, Android phones and Android tablets.

apps.name: City Rush
apps.tagline: Pick up a fare. Drop it off. Go again.
apps.summary: A top-down arcade driving game with two ways to play on the same city: an endless Rush Hour score attack, and a twelve-mission Career.
long: Rush Hour is one loop with no menus in the middle of it. A shift starts at 45 seconds, and reaching a pickup or completing a drop-off banks time sized to the leg you just drove — so a long haul funds itself and a short hop does not. The run ends when the clock does.

Every delivery raises a streak multiplier up to ×10. Every crash resets it to ×1 and costs two seconds, which makes driving clean the actual skill. Finish a fare without touching anything and it pays 25% extra before the multiplier applies.

Ambient traffic circulates the grid on correct right-hand lanes and picks turns at intersections. Hitting one is a crash; sliding past one at speed is a near miss, which pays cash and banks nitro. Coins sit in the driving lanes, so the greedy line and the fast line rarely match.
features: Rush Hour
An endless score-attack shift. Two taps from launch to driving, and it lasts as long as you keep earning time.
Career
Twelve stage-driven missions on the same city, reached from the home screen.
Streak multiplier
Up to ×10 for clean driving, reset to ×1 by any crash.
Near misses
Sliding past traffic at speed pays cash and banks nitro. Hitting it does not.
Emergent session length
A bad shift is 40 seconds, a good one runs several minutes. Nothing asks you to commit up front.
Difficulty that ramps
Time is granted less generously and traffic thickens with every delivery, instead of a hard timer cutting you off.

apps.name: Keyclave
apps.summary: An offline, encrypted vault for the documents that matter — passports, licences, insurance, medical records, titles, warranties and contracts. Nothing leaves your device, because there is nowhere for it to go.
long: Every document is encrypted with its own key, and those keys are wrapped by a master key derived from your password. Unlock with a password, a six-digit PIN, Face ID or Touch ID, with a 160-bit recovery key as a fallback.

Text inside your documents is recognized on-device with Apple's Vision framework, so search covers what a document says and not just what you named it. Filter by category, tag, date, expiration and document type.
There is no networking code anywhere in the project — no analytics, no logging, no third-party SDKs and no cloud sync. The privacy claim is a property of the build, not a promise in a policy.
features: Per-file encryption
AES-256-GCM with a per-document key, wrapped by a master key derived from your password.
Unlock how you like
Password or six-digit PIN, plus optional Face ID and Touch ID, with a recovery key as a fallback.
On-device OCR
Apple Vision reads the text in your documents so search finds what they actually say.
Organized how you think
Thirteen categories, unlimited user-defined tags, and filters for date, expiration and type.
Save to Vault
A share extension so documents can go straight into the vault from anywhere in the system.
Expiration reminders
Local notifications before a passport, licence or policy runs out. Scheduled on-device.

privacy.headline: Keyclave collects nothing. There is no account, no server and no analytics — and no networking code in the app at all.
stored: Encrypted, in the app's private storage on your device
They are the point of the app
So search and history work offline
The device Keychain, marked “when unlocked, this device only”
So biometric unlock works without storing your password
So repeated failed attempts still count after a relaunch
To remember how you like the app configured
permissions: Face ID / Touch ID (optional)
To unlock the vault without typing your password. The biometric check happens in Apple's secure hardware; the app never receives your biometric data.
Camera (optional)
Only to scan a paper document into the vault when you choose to. Scans are processed on-device and stored encrypted.
Photo Library (optional)
Only to import a photo you select into the vault.
Notifications (optional)
For expiration reminders you set. Scheduled locally on your device — no push server is involved.
privacy.network: There is none. The app contains no URLSession, no network connections and no web views that load remote content. It cannot upload your documents, and there is no service to upload them to.
privacy.third_parties: None. The project declares zero external dependencies — no CocoaPods, no Carthage, no remote Swift packages, no analytics and no crash reporting. Only Apple's own frameworks are used.
privacy.extra: Your master password is never stored anywhere — not on the device and not with us. That means we cannot recover your vault if you lose both your password and your recovery key. That is the trade-off that makes the encryption meaningful.

faq: What happens if I forget my password?
Use your recovery key. If you have lost both, the vault cannot be opened — by you or by us. Your master password is never stored anywhere, which is what makes the encryption real.
Is my vault backed up to iCloud?
No. There is no cloud sync of any kind. Use the app's own encrypted export if you want a backup, and store it somewhere you control.
Can Flowlab Apps read my documents?
No. We have no server, no account system and no key. There is nothing on our side to read.
Does search work offline?
Yes. Text recognition runs on your device with Apple's Vision framework, and the index is stored encrypted alongside your documents.
How do I add a document from another app?
Use the Share sheet and pick “Save to Vault”.
Which devices are supported?
iPhone running iOS 17 or later, and Mac running macOS 14 or later.

apps.name: Keybound
apps.tagline: A password manager with no account and no server.
apps.summary: A local-first password manager for macOS, iOS and Android. There is no account, no server and no sync service. Your vault is a single encrypted file on your device, and the only thing that opens it is your master password.
long: Argon2id at 64 MiB and t=3 derives your key; XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts the vault. Envelope encryption means a random vault master key encrypts the body, and each unlock method — password, recovery key, biometric — stores its own wrapped copy, so adding a recovery key never weakens the password path.
All cryptography lives in Rust. The interface receives decrypted entries only when it needs them, and never the master key, TOTP seeds or passkey private keys.

Two devices sync directly to each other over your own local network, authenticated with an ephemeral key exchange and a six-digit code you confirm on both screens. There is no relay and no server in the middle, because none exists.
features: Modern cryptography
Argon2id key derivation and XChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, with envelope-wrapped unlock methods.
Everything in one vault
Logins, TOTP codes, secure notes, cards, identities, SSH keys, API keys, licences and recovery keys.
Password health
A dashboard for weak, reused and stale credentials, plus a generator.
Opt-in breach checking
Uses k-anonymity: only the first five characters of a password's hash ever leave your device.
Import from anywhere
Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePassXC, LastPass and browser CSV exports, plus encrypted export and import.
Direct device sync
LAN sync with QR pairing and a six-digit verification code. No relay, no cloud, no account.

privacy.headline: Keybound collects nothing. There is no sign-up, no email address, no device identifier, no usage analytics, no crash reporting and no advertising.
stored: A single encrypted file in the app's private storage on your device
It holds your logins, notes, cards and keys
Your device's keychain or keystore, protected by biometric hardware
So Face ID or a fingerprint can unlock the vault
Auto-lock timing, theme and similar settings
Wherever you choose to put them, encrypted with the same scheme
So you can keep a copy you control
permissions: Biometrics (optional)
Face ID, Touch ID or Android biometric unlock. The check happens in your device's secure hardware, and the key is invalidated automatically if your enrolled biometrics change.
Camera (optional)
Only to scan a QR code when pairing two of your own devices for sync, or to capture a TOTP setup code.
Local network (optional)
Only when you sync two of your own devices, and only for the duration of that sync.
privacy.network: Two connections exist, both under your control. **Breach checking is opt-in**: when you run it, a SHA-1 hash is computed on your device and only the first five hexadecimal characters are sent to api.pwnedpasswords.com, which replies with hundreds of matching prefixes; the comparison happens on your device. The service never receives your password, your full hash, or anything identifying you. **Device sync is peer-to-peer**: your two devices connect directly over your own local network, authenticated by an ephemeral P-256 key exchange and a short code you confirm on both screens. There is no relay and no copy retained anywhere.
privacy.third_parties: Have I Been Pwned (api.pwnedpasswords.com) receives a five-character hash prefix, and only if you choose to run a breach check. Their handling of that request is governed by their own privacy policy. If you never run a breach check, the app never contacts them. There are no other third parties, no analytics libraries and no advertising SDKs.
privacy.store_note: One qualification, for completeness: if you run the optional breach check, five hexadecimal characters of a password's SHA-1 hash are sent to Have I Been Pwned. That prefix matches hundreds of unrelated passwords, cannot identify you or the password it came from, is never seen or stored by us, and is only ever sent when you ask for the check. That is why the declarations above still read **no data collected**. Section 4 describes it in full.
privacy.extra: Your master password is never stored — not on your device and not anywhere else. We have no server holding your data, no account system and no way to identify you. We could not hand over your vault if we were asked to, because we do not have it.

faq: What happens if I forget my master password?
Use your recovery key. Without either, the vault cannot be opened by anyone, including us. That is the point.
Is there a cloud sync?
No. Devices sync directly to each other over your local network, with a code you confirm on both screens.
What exactly gets sent during a breach check?
The first five characters of a password's SHA-1 hash, and nothing else. The service returns hundreds of candidate hashes and the match is computed on your device.
Can I import from another password manager?
Yes — Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePassXC, LastPass and browser CSV exports are supported.
Where does the encryption happen?
In Rust, on your device. The interface never receives the master key, TOTP seeds or passkey private keys.
Which platforms are supported?
macOS, iOS and Android.

apps.name: Universal Remote
apps.tagline: Your phone, as the remote you actually lost.
apps.summary: A remote control app that finds compatible TVs and streaming devices on your Wi-Fi, pairs with them, and loads the right remote layout automatically.
long: Discovery finds supported devices on your local network, identifies the manufacturer, walks you through whatever pairing the TV requires, and then shows a remote built for that device rather than a generic grid of buttons.
Multiple TVs in the same household are supported, and paired devices are remembered so the second launch is instant.

Where a manufacturer has closed off local control, the app says so plainly instead of showing a button that silently does nothing. Adapters for Google TV / Android TV, Samsung, LG and Vizio are in progress.
This app is early in development and is not yet available in either store.
features: Automatic discovery
Finds compatible devices on your Wi-Fi and identifies what they are.
Guided pairing
Walks through whatever approval the TV asks for on screen.
The right layout, automatically
Loads a remote built for the device you connected to, not a lowest-common-denominator grid.
Multiple devices
Remembers paired and favorite devices across several TVs in one household.
Honest about limits
When a function or a device is unsupported, it says so rather than failing quietly.
Local only
Commands go straight from your phone to your TV over your own network.

privacy.headline: Universal Remote collects no data. It talks to your TV over your own network and to nothing else.
stored: So you do not have to re-pair every launch
Pairing tokens issued by your TV
So the TV keeps trusting this phone
To remember your layout and settings
permissions: Local network
To discover TVs on your Wi-Fi and send them commands. Nothing about your network is sent off your device.
privacy.network: Traffic goes from your phone directly to your TV on your own local network. There is no account, no cloud service and no server operated by Flowlab Apps involved in controlling a device.
privacy.third_parties: None. No analytics SDKs, advertising libraries or trackers are included.
privacy.store_note: Universal Remote does send network traffic — commands to a television on your own Wi-Fi. That traffic stays inside your home network, never reaches a server operated by us, and carries nothing about you, which is why the declarations above read **no data collected**.
privacy.extra: The app does not read your viewing history, does not know what you are watching, and does not inventory the other devices on your network beyond the televisions it is looking for.

faq: Is this available yet?
Not yet. Universal Remote is early in development and has not been released to either store.
Why can't the app find my TV?
Both devices must be on the same Wi-Fi network, and the TV must have network control enabled. Some manufacturers now disable it by default.
Why are some buttons unavailable?
Because that television does not expose that function to third-party apps. The app shows what is genuinely available rather than pretending.
Does it work over Bluetooth or infrared?
No. Control is over Wi-Fi, which is what the supported platforms expose to third-party apps.
Which TVs are supported?
Adapters for Google TV / Android TV, Samsung, LG and Vizio are in progress. The supported list will be published before release.

apps.name: Matla
apps.tagline: Ramadan, prayer and Quran. Calm, offline, private.
apps.summary: Matla is a companion for a Muslim's daily worship: a Ramadan fasting countdown for suhoor and iftar, prayer times with reliable reminders, a Qibla compass and an offline Quran. Everything is calculated on your phone. There are no accounts, no ads, no analytics and no servers.
long: During Ramadan, Matla shows whether you are fasting right now, how long until suhoor ends and how long until iftar, with a countdown on your Lock Screen and Dynamic Island on iOS and on the home screen on both platforms. Reminders for suhoor, Fajr, iftar and each prayer are scheduled on your device.

Prayer times are computed locally from your location (or a city you pick) using a calculation method you choose. The method, madhab and any high-latitude rule are always shown on screen, because authorities legitimately differ and your mosque may follow a different convention.
The Quran reader works fully offline with the Uthmani text from the Tanzil project and an English translation by Talal Itani. Bookmarks, your last-read position and search stay on the device.
Matla is a worship companion, not a source of religious rulings. Hijri dates and the start of Ramadan are shown as estimates until you confirm the announcement for your region.
features: Ramadan fasting countdown
Suhoor and iftar countdowns derived from Fajr and Maghrib for your location, with a fasting-day ring, Live Activity and home screen widgets.
Prayer times and reminders
Five daily prayers plus sunrise, with per-prayer reminders and adhan sounds. Exact alarms on Android so reminders fire on time.
Transparent calculation settings
Choose the calculation authority, Asr madhab, high-latitude rule and per-prayer offsets. The active method is always visible.
Qibla compass
Direction to the Kaaba from your location, with a numeric bearing, accuracy indicator and calibration guidance.
Offline Quran
Uthmani Arabic text with an English translation, bookmarks, last-read position and search, with no download required.
Hijri calendar
Today's Hijri date with an adjustment for local moon sighting, and notable dates marked as estimates.

privacy.headline: Matla keeps everything on your device. Your location never leaves your phone. There are no accounts, no ads, no analytics and no servers.
stored: To compute prayer times, fasting times and the Qibla direction
To remember how you like the app configured
Your private Ramadan record; nothing is shared
So you can continue where you stopped
permissions: Location (while using the app, approximate)

To compute prayer times, fasting times and the Qibla direction for where you are. Matla asks only for approximate accuracy and only while the app is open, never in the background. You can decline it and pick a city from the built-in offline list instead.
Notifications
For prayer, suhoor and iftar reminders. Everything is scheduled on your device; nothing goes through a push server.
Exact alarms (Android)
So a reminder fires at the exact minute rather than whenever the system gets around to it. Android may ask you to allow this in Settings.
Run at startup (Android)
So reminders you already scheduled survive a device restart.
Compass and motion sensors
To point the Qibla compass. Sensor readings are used on the device and never stored or sent anywhere.
privacy.network: Version 1 of Matla makes no network requests at all. Prayer times, the Hijri calendar, the Qibla direction and the Quran text are all computed or stored on the device. If a later version adds streamed Quran audio, it will fetch audio files from a content server; that request contains the file requested and nothing about you, and this policy will be updated before that version ships.
privacy.third_parties: None. There are no analytics SDKs, advertising libraries, crash reporters or trackers in the app.
privacy.store_note: Because location is processed only on the device and never transmitted, both stores treat it as not collected.

faq: Why do my prayer times differ from my mosque?

Prayer times are calculated from your location using the authority you select in Settings. Mosques often apply their own precaution minutes or a different convention for Fajr and Isha. Matla shows the active method on screen so you can compare, and per-prayer offsets let you match your local timetable.
Why is the Ramadan start date marked as estimated?

The Hijri calendar in Matla follows the calculated Umm al-Qura calendar. Many communities begin Ramadan on a confirmed moon sighting, which can differ by a day. Matla asks you to confirm the announced date for your region and lets you adjust the Hijri date by a day either way.
Does the fast start at imsak or at Fajr?
The fast begins at Fajr. Some communities stop eating a few minutes earlier as a precaution; Matla can show that imsak line if you turn it on, and labels it as precautionary.
Do I need an account or an internet connection?
No. There is no sign-up and no login, and every feature in version 1 works offline.
Reminders are late or missing on Android.

Some Android phones stop apps from scheduling exact alarms to save battery. Matla includes a reminder self-test and step-by-step guidance for your phone brand in Settings. Allowing exact alarms and turning off battery optimisation for Matla fixes most cases.
Where is my data stored?
On your device only. Deleting the app removes its local data, subject to your device's own backup and restore settings.
Which platforms are supported?
iPhone and Android. iOS additionally supports Live Activities on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island.
